avoided_actions.rationale: MG is a peripheral neuromuscular junction disorder; EEG has no diagnostic role.
No CSF role in MG; LP risks complications without diagnostic yield.
Advanced imaging (PET/MR spectroscopy/perfusion) is not indicated for MG diagnosis or staging; CT chest covers thymoma screening.
Echocardiography is not indicated for MG unless a comorbid cardiac question exists.
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated for MG unless arrhythmia or autonomic disease is independently suspected.

accepted: Myasthenia gravis, AChR antibody-positive, generalized (MGFA Class IIb), paraneoplastic in context of peripheral T-cell lymphoma; concurrent vincristine-induced peripheral neuropathy as a separate process

differential.key_features: Vincristine can cause distal sensorimotor neuropathy but does NOT produce fatigable ptosis, diplopia, or RNS decrement; both processes coexist here.
Lymphomas are uncommon causes of LEMS; baseline CMAPs and high-rate RNS facilitation pattern would clarify; here AChR positive suggests MG.
Steroids in EPOCH could cause proximal myopathy but not fatigable bulbar weakness or RNS decrement.
Generalized fatigue from chemo is expected but does not produce focal fatigable cranial signs.
No mass lesion on brain MRI; CSF and imaging not supportive.

key_clinical_evidence: Fluctuating, fatigable weakness with diurnal pattern (worse evening) is the clinical hallmark of MG — fixed weakness suggests an alternative diagnosis.
Ocular involvement (ptosis, diplopia) is asymmetric and fatigable in MG; thyroid eye disease causes restrictive (not fatigable) ophthalmoplegia.
Single-fiber EMG (sensitivity >95%) is the most sensitive electrodiagnostic test — order when RNS is non-diagnostic or serology is negative.
All confirmed MG cases require CT chest for thymoma — present in roughly 10-15% of generalized MG; thymectomy (MGTX trial) improves long-term outcomes in non-thymoma AChR+ MG as well.
Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, telithromycin, IV magnesium, and neuromuscular blockers can precipitate myasthenic crisis and must be screened against any new prescription.
Vincristine peripheral neuropathy and MG are clinically distinguishable: vincristine → distal stocking-glove sensory loss; MG → fatigable proximal/bulbar weakness.
Active malignancy + immunosuppression: steroid-sparing strategies and infection control influence MG treatment selection.

patient.chief_complaint: New bilateral ptosis and diplopia in a patient on chemotherapy for lymphoma

medications.drug: Dose-adjusted EPOCH (etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin)

past_medical_history: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma (high-grade, stage IV) — receiving EPOCH chemotherapy, currently after cycle 4 of 6
Prior ICU admission for severe sepsis during chemotherapy cycle 2

patient.history_present_illness: A 57-year-old man with high-grade peripheral T-cell lymphoma receiving EPOCH chemotherapy (after 4 of 6 planned cycles) presented with new bilateral ptosis and diplopia over 5 weeks. He had been doing well on chemotherapy with near-complete metabolic response on interim PET-CT, but his oncology team noted new drooping of his left eyelid at a clinic visit. The patient confirmed the ptosis had been present for 5 weeks and was progressive. He developed horizontal diplopia 3 weeks ago, initially intermittent and worse after a long day, and now present during most of his waking hours. He also reported jaw fatigue when eating — he rested between bites during meal times. His voice had become increasingly nasal, a change his wife noted clearly. He denied significant dysphagia. He had been attributing all new neurological symptoms to chemotherapy toxicity, which had already caused peripheral neuropathy from vincristine. He had multiple prior episodes of febrile neutropenia requiring hospitalization and had a severe sepsis episode after his second cycle requiring one week in the ICU. His oncologist was concerned about: (1) central nervous system lymphoma invasion, (2) paraneoplastic syndrome, (3) chemotherapy neurotoxicity (vincristine-induced cranial neuropathy), and (4) opportunistic infection. Brain MRI was performed and reported as showing no CNS lymphoma. He was referred to neurology for NMJ evaluation after the oncologist noted the fatigable pattern was inconsistent with typical vincristine neuropathy, which causes peripheral sensorimotor neuropathy rather than cranial neuropathy with fatigability.

neurological_exam.additional: NIF -48 cmH2O (borderline). No dysphagia currently. Mild jaw fatigue on eating. Oncology team suspected chemotherapy neurotoxicity — vincristine peripheral neuropathy confirmed but does not explain all findings.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Bilateral ptosis, left greater than right. Levator excursion left 7mm, right 10mm. Fatigable ptosis on sustained upgaze (left eye complete at 50 seconds). Horizontal diplopia on leftward gaze. Limited left eye adduction. Pupils equal, reactive. Facial weakness bilateral. Voice nasal after sustained speech.
neurological_exam.gait: Mildly broad-based. Steppage pattern bilaterally (vincristine neuropathy).
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Mildly fatigued appearance. Normal language. Mildly slowed processing from chemotherapy-related fatigue.
neurological_exam.motor: Proximal upper extremity weakness: deltoids 4/5 bilaterally. Hip flexors 4/5. Distal strength intact. Deep tendon reflexes: 1+ throughout — mildly hyporeflexic (chemotherapy-related). Fatigable weakness documented on exam.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 1+ throughout (mild hyporeflexia — vincristine neuropathy). Plantar downgoing.
neurological_exam.sensory: Mild stocking-glove diminished sensation feet (vincristine peripheral neuropathy).
